questions.question: The EU AI Act's 'systemic-risk GPAI' tier is defined by which threshold?
options: Models with more than 100 billion parameters
Models trained with more than 1e25 FLOP of compute
Models deployed to more than 1 million users in the EU
Models that score above the 95th percentile on MMLU
questions.explanation: The EU AI Act's systemic-risk GPAI tier applies to general-purpose AI models trained with more than 1e25 FLOP of compute. This threshold is estimated to bind 5-15 companies globally as of 2026. Systemic-risk GPAI providers have additional obligations beyond the baseline GPAI requirements.

questions.question: When did EU AI Act's prohibited practices (Article 5) and AI literacy obligations begin applying?
options: 1 August 2024 — when the Act entered force
2 February 2025 — the first applicability date after the Act's entry into force
2 August 2025 — when GPAI obligations apply
2 August 2026 — full applicability date
questions.explanation: The EU AI Act entered force on 1 August 2024, but most provisions apply on a phased timeline. Prohibited practices (Article 5) and AI literacy obligations were the first to apply, on 2 February 2025 (6 months after entry into force). GPAI obligations follow on 2 August 2025; full applicability including Article 50 transparency is 2 August 2026.

questions.question: The GPAI Code of Practice (published 10 July 2025) has three chapters. Which chapter applies only to systemic-risk GPAI providers?
options: Transparency
Copyright
Safety and Security
Governance and Accountability
questions.explanation: The GPAI Code of Practice's three chapters: Transparency (all GPAI providers), Copyright (all GPAI providers), and Safety and Security (systemic-risk GPAI providers only). Enforcement begins August 2026; until then good-faith compliance is accepted.

questions.question: What does the renaming of UK AISI to 'AI Security Institute' (February 2025) signal about policy direction?
options: The UK is expanding its focus from AI security to a broader safety remit
The rebrand narrows scope: dropping algorithmic bias and free-speech framings to focus on frontier capability security, aligned with the UK's post-Brexit industrial strategy
The rename reflects a merger with the UK cybersecurity agency NCSC
The AI Security Institute is now a regulatory body with enforcement powers unlike the former advisory AISI
questions.explanation: The February 2025 rename from 'AI Safety Institute' to 'AI Security Institute' deliberately narrows scope: it drops algorithmic bias and free-speech safety framings to focus specifically on frontier capability security threats. The UK AISI also open-sourced the Inspect evaluation tool and collaborates with Redwood on control safety cases.

questions.question: Korea's AI Framework Act (effective January 2026) includes which provision specifically targeting foreign AI companies?
options: Foreign AI models must be retrained on Korean language data before deployment
Foreign AI companies must designate local representatives in Korea for regulatory accountability
Foreign AI companies must pay a licensing fee to the Korean MSIT
AI models from countries with no AI regulatory framework are prohibited from operating in Korea
questions.explanation: Korea's AI Framework Act (passed December 2024, effective January 2026) mandates that foreign AI companies operating in Korea designate local representatives — analogous to GDPR's local representative requirements. This ensures Korean regulators have a contact point for enforcement and compliance questions.

questions.question: For a company operating in multiple jurisdictions simultaneously, which regulatory framework generally sets the highest compliance floor in 2026?
options: US CAISI standards, because they are the most technically precise
UK AI Security Institute guidance, because it is the most operationally detailed
EU AI Act, because it has the strictest risk-tiered requirements and highest penalties (up to 15M EUR or 3% global turnover)
Korean AI Framework Act, because it has the broadest coverage of AI system types
questions.explanation: The EU AI Act is the strictest among the four regimes discussed: mandatory risk tiers, conformity assessments for high-risk systems, GPAI code of practice, Article 50 transparency requirements, and penalties up to 15M EUR or 3% of global annual turnover. Deployers in multiple jurisdictions must comply with the strictest applicable standard, which in 2026 is typically the EU AI Act.
